coordination_failures: Extremely low resource utilization (12.5%) despite high request volume (76 requests, only 17 granted).
Repeated rejections for road repair (8 times) likely delayed access and compounded losses in later missions.
Critical resource exhaustion (ambulances, fire engines, repair crews) indicates poor allocation forecasting.
Late-spawning missions (m8–m9) faced constrained assets due to earlier overcommitment.
headline: Efficient Early Response Saves Lives Despite Resource Shortages

key_moments.description: First wave of high-severity missions (m1–m3) resolved, saving 54 lives with only 12 lost.
Second disaster wave hits; simultaneous fires, medical surges, and infrastructure failures strain resources.
Longest mission (m7) resolves after 6 ticks, highlighting response delays in hospital district fire.
Final missions (m8–m9) conclude just before simulation end, with m9 achieving zero fatalities.

lessons: Pre-position critical resources based on early incident severity to avoid mid-crisis shortages.
Prioritize road repair approvals to maintain access for ambulances and fire crews.
Balance rapid initial response with sustainable resource reserves for secondary disaster waves.
Track and act on rejection patterns to adjust coordination protocols in real time.
Improve dispatch logic to reduce average response time below 4.44 ticks for higher survival rates.
what_worked: All 9 missions were resolved with zero failures, indicating strong operational follow-through.
Early missions (m1–m3) were resolved within 4 ticks, minimizing initial casualties.
Low panic level (0.050) suggests effective public communication and visible response efforts.
High lives saved-to-lost ratio (3:1) reflects prioritization of life-preserving actions.
